post.description:
Use when the user wants a team's or league's gear or a department within it. league_id comes from a search facet (type o), team_id from list_teams, department_id from a facet option of type d. Pass url instead of ids to follow a facet or breadcrumb path returned by this function or search_products.

<!-- aisa-pricing:start -->
按用量计费；默认请求预估费用：$0.0005 USD（不是固定价格）。 声明的单位费率：每 firecrawl_credit $0.0001 USD。 最终费用以账户适用价格及实际结算为准。
<!-- aisa-pricing:end -->

department_id.description: Fanatics department id (the d- segment), e.g. 8019 = Sweatshirts; from a facet option of type d.

include_facets.description: Include the site's facet groups (leagues, departments, players, brands, price bands) with their option URLs. Set false for a smaller result when only the products matter.

league_id.description: Fanatics league/org id (the o- segment), e.g. 23 = NBA, 25 = NFL, 19 = MLB, 5 = College.

page.description: 1-based page number (the site's pageNumber).

page_size.description: Products per page (the site's pageSize). The storefront UI offers 24, 48, 72 and 96.

sort.description: Sort order (the site's sortOption values).

team_id.description: Fanatics team id (the t- segment), e.g. 3356 = Atlanta Hawks; from list_teams.

url.description: A www.fanatics.com listing URL or path (from a facet option, breadcrumb or the address bar). Mutually exclusive with the id inputs.

Missteps in firestop specification can compromise compartmentation strategies, increase liability risks, and result in costly remediation during construction or later in the building’s life cycle. If a fire breaks out at a commercial property, commercial firestopping can compartmentalize or confine the fire and keep it from spreading through the entire building. At Division 7, Inc., our highly trained professionals understand how important commercial-grade firestopping is for protecting lives and property. Division 7, Inc. provides quality firestop and insulation systems by offering a complete range of commercial and residential insulation services that can be individually tailored to your specific needs. response.text:
WARNING LETTER
WL # 724202

September 14, 2026

Dear Mr. Bonnell:

You registered your facility with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an outsourcing facility under section 503B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) [21 U.S.C. § 353b]1 on December 13, 2013, and most recently on December 5, 2025. From October 20, 2025, to October 30, 2025, an FDA investigator inspected your facility, SCA Pharmaceuticals, LLC located at 8821 Knoedl Court, Little Rock, Arkansas 72205. During the inspection, the investigator noted serious deficiencies in your practices for producing drug products intended or expected to be sterile, which put patients at risk.

FDA issued a Form FDA 483 to your facility on October 30, 2025. We reviewed your November 21, 2025, and December 31, 2025, responses to our Form FDA 483 in detail and acknowledge receipt of your subsequent correspondence. Based on this inspection, it appears you produced drugs that violate the FDCA.

A. Compounded Drug Products under the FDCA

Under section 503B(b) of the FDCA, a compounder can register as an outsourcing facility with FDA. Drug products compounded by or under the direct supervision of a licensed pharmacist in an outsourcing facility qualify for exemptions from the drug approval requirements in section 505 of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 355(a)], the requirement in section 502(f)(1) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 352(f)(1)] that labeling bear adequate directions for use and the Drug Supply Chain Security Act requirements in section 582 of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 360eee-1] if the conditions in section 503B of the FDCA are met.

An outsourcing facility, which is defined in section 503B(d)(4) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 353b(d)(4)], is a facility at one geographic location or address that — (i) is engaged in the compounding of sterile drugs; (ii) has elected to register as an outsourcing facility; and (iii) complies with all of the requirements of this section. Outsourcing facilities must comply with other applicable provisions of the FDCA, including section 501(a)(2)(B) [21 U.S.C. § 351(a)(2)(B)], regarding current good manufacturing practice (CGMP), and section 501(a)(2)(A) [21 U.S.C. § 351(a)(2)(A)], regarding insanitary conditions. Generally, CGMP requirements for the preparation of drug products are established in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) parts 210 and 211.

B. Violations of the FDCA

Adulterated Drug Products

The FDA investigator collected evidence indicating that drug products intended or expected to be sterile were prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions, whereby they may have become contaminated with filth or rendered injurious to health, causing your drug products to be adulterated under section 501(a)(2)(A) of the FDCA. For example, the investigator collected evidence indicating that:

1. Your facility lacked routine and rigorous certification of the ISO 5 areas, including airflow visualization studies performed under dynamic conditions.

2. Your firm did not perform adequate product evaluation and take appropriate corrective action after microbial contamination was recovered within the ISO 5 aseptic processing area.

3. Your component control is not adequately designed or maintained to prevent contamination of product contact surfaces due to the presence of foreign (unusual) material between the stopper ribs of syringes.

4. Your compounding technicians and aseptic assistants employ poor practices which introduce risk of microbial contamination into the ISO 5 classified critical areas during production of drugs intended to be sterile.

For example, during the production of Fentanyl Citrate 2 mcg/mL Bupivacaine HCl 0.125% lot #1125035913 and/or Methadone HCl 10 mg/mL lot #1125035922, your compounding technicians:

a. Moved quickly in a critical area or in an area immediately adjacent to a critical area such that unidirectional airflow is likely to be disrupted.

b. Leaned into the hood, allowing their head and upper body to enter the ISO 5 classified critical area, thereby disrupting unidirectional airflow.

c. Blocked first pass air by placing gloved hands directly over the following:

i. Hanging IV bag ports when making sterile connections.

ii. The IV bag ports when disinfecting prior to filling.

iii. The open filled syringes and the syringe cap trays during the process of screwing caps onto the syringes.

d. Conducted aseptic operations on or directly above the hood deck surface in vertical flow hoods, which prevents unidirectional first air with minimal turbulence from surrounding aseptic operations during sterile connections and filling of drug products intended or expected to be sterile into open sterile containers.

e. Regularly rested their arms on the work surface of the hood during aseptic production. This practice may introduce contamination into the ISO 5 work area.

Additionally, your aseptic assistants:

a. Moved quickly in an area immediately adjacent to a critical area such that unidirectional airflow is likely to be disrupted.

b. Used disinfectant in a manner insufficient to achieve adequate levels of disinfection of materials, such as the IV bag ports, during transfer into the ISO 5 classified critical areas by spraying very quickly or from a significant distance or failing to treat both sides of the IV bags. Prior to disinfection, aseptic assistants regularly touched the IV bag ports in the ISO 7 area with their gloved hands.

5. Your environmental monitoring program lacks adequate routine environmental monitoring that captures data representative of aseptic production conditions. For example, during the production of Fentanyl Citrate 2 mcg/mL Bupivacaine HCl 0.125% lot #1125035913:

a. The active air sampler is placed to the far right of the hood instead of adjacent to the areas where aseptic operations occur, including the left and center portions of the ISO 5 classified hood.

b. Compounding technicians do not always carefully roll their individual fingers across the media touch plate during personnel monitoring. The compounding technician quickly touched each fingertip to the media plates instead of methodically rolling their fingertips.

6. Your firm failed to perform adequate airflow visualization studies under dynamic conditions to demonstrate unidirectional airflow within the ISO 5 area. Your airflow visualization studies are deficient because:

a. The studies do not clearly demonstrate that the airflow pattern sweeps over and away from the critical areas near and on the ISO 5 classified LAF hood work surface where aseptic operations occur. Instead, the smoke appears to arc out of the hood significantly higher than the critical area and then travel up toward the ceiling in the surrounding ISO 7 classified area.

b. In your most recent airflow visualization study VAL-25-044-FR, you indicated that (b)(4) people are allowed in ISO 7 (b)(4) Room (b)(4) during aseptic operations; however, the smoke study videos provided during the FDA inspection only include a maximum of (b)(4) people, and fail to demonstrate that airflow patterns inside the ISO 5 classified critical areas are not impacted by a large number of personnel moving inside cleanroom Room (b)(4).

The FDA investigator also collected evidence indicating CGMP violations at your facility, that caused your drug products to be adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FDCA. The violations include, for example:

1. Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures that are designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile, and that include validation of all aseptic and sterilization processes (21 CFR 211.113(b)).

2. Your firm failed to establish an adequate air supply filtered through high-efficiency particulate air filters under positive pressure in the aseptic processing areas (21 CFR 211.42(c)(10)(iii)).

3. Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192).

4. Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures designed to assure that components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling, and drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)).

5. Your firm failed to establish adequate written responsibilities and procedures applicable to the quality control unit and to follow written procedures applicable to the quality control unit (21 CFR 211.22(d)). Specifically, our review of the data collected during the inspection revealed that your firm does not maintain the production video recordings which are used to determine root causes and corrective actions during investigations. For example, after recovering microbial contamination inside the ISO 5 classified critical area during the production of Ketamine HCl 10 mg/mL lot 1125035065, your Quality Unit evaluated the production video recording as part of excursion investigation EXC-2025-0045 to examine aseptic practices for potential root causes. However, instead of retaining the video recording as a quality related document, you only retained still images. Your Chief Quality Officer stated that video recordings are kept for approximately (b)(4) before being overwritten.

Outsourcing facilities must comply with CGMP requirements under section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FDCA. FDA’s regulations regarding CGMP requirements for the preparation of drug products have been established in 21 CFR parts 210 and 211. FDA intends to promulgate more specific CGMP regulations for outsourcing facilities. FDA has issued a revised draft guidance, Current Good Manufacturing Practice — Guidance for Human Drug Compounding Outsourcing Facilities under Section 503B of the FD&C Act. This draft guidance, when finalized, will describe FDA’s expectations regarding outsourcing facilities and the CGMP requirements in 21 CFR parts 210 and 211 until more specific CGMP regulations for outsourcing facilities are promulgated.

Under section 301(a) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(a)], the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce of any drug that is adulterated is a prohibited act. Further, it is also a prohibited act under section 301(k) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(k)] to do any act with respect to a drug, if such act is done while the drug is held for sale after shipment in interstate commerce and results in the drug being adulterated.

C. Corrective Actions

We have reviewed your facility’s responses to the Form FDA 483 dated November 21, 2025, and December 31, 2025.

Some of your corrective actions appear adequate. However, we are unable to fully evaluate some of your corrective actions due to lack of adequate supporting documentation:

1. Although you stated that you performed airflow visualization studies in all (b)(4) hoods, you did not clearly demonstrate that these studies were performed in all (b)(4) hoods during the most recent airflow visualization assessment, performed in 2025. Additionally, while you concluded that the hoods are identical and therefore functionally equivalent, this approach does not account for potential variations in the HEPA filter performance, for example, resulting from particulate accumulation over time, nor the impact of physical placement of hoods within the room—including proximity to doors, return vents, and other environmental factors that may affect airflow where production activities are occurring.

Some of your corrective actions appear deficient:

1. You did not demonstrate that the probable root cause of inadequate material sanitization had no impact on the released portions of the batch associated with microbial excursions in the ISO 5 classified areas during production. You indicated both in your investigations and in your response that your material sanitization process is robust, but also concluded that the microbial contamination was most likely due to inadequate material sanitization.

You failed to demonstrate that microbial contamination was not present in the materials associated with the released portions of the batch. You did not demonstrate that the material sanitization process for the released portions of the batches did not include the same deficiencies as the material sanitization for the rejected portion of the batch. Further, you failed to initiate any corrective and preventative action plans to determine whether you need to improve your material sanitization process to prevent reoccurrence.

2. It appears that your visual inspection system is inadequate because you classify particulate defects as major and therefore only characterize and investigate the observed particles when the defect rate is above the major defect threshold of (b)(4)%. Extrinsic particulates should be classified as critical, and the intrinsic particulates should be evaluated based on multiple factors, including particle size and route of administration, to determine the appropriate defect classification. Your SOP ILP-001-LR, Product Inspection and Defect Classification, states, “If a DRL (Defect Rate Limit) threshold is exceeded related to ‘Particulate/material in solution,’ the particulate/material must be identified during the event.” According to your visual inspection data, you detected between (b)(4) and (b)(4) particles in (b)(4) separate lots between April 2025 and September 2025, only (b)(4) lots of which exceeded the (b)(4)% threshold for major defects. According to your Deviation log, only (b)(4) defect incidents were investigated between April 2025 and September 2025, and these were related to any Defect Rate Limit Threshold Exceedance, not just those involving particles. Therefore, you do not have an adequate system in place to ensure that you identify and appropriately investigate contaminating particles.

3. You did not commit to revising the minor defect classification for “[f]oreign (unusual) material, e.g., cardboard trapped between stopper ribs” to account for the criticality of the foreign material. While you noted that any units exhibiting this defect are rejected, the defect rate limit applied to minor defects ((b)(4)%) is not appropriate for adequately investigating, trending, and performing corrective actions, as necessary, to mitigate this contamination risk.

You did not provide adequate documentation to demonstrate that foreign materials are contained within the ribs of the syringe stoppers in non-product-contact area and will not pose contamination risks to the drug product. In addition, the syringe filling process demonstrates that the foreign material does come into contact with product-contact area of the syringes. For example, any cardboard particles trapped within the syringe ribs may be pressed against the inner syringe wall during filling, potentially introducing particles onto a surface that subsequently contacts the drug product solution.

In addition to the issues discussed above, you should note that CGMP requires the implementation of quality oversight and controls over the manufacture of drugs, including the safety of raw materials, materials used in drug manufacturing, and finished drug products. See section 501 of the FDCA. If you choose to contract with a laboratory to perform some functions required by CGMP, it is essential that you select a qualified contractor and that you maintain sufficient oversight of the contractor’s operations to ensure that it is fully CGMP compliant. Regardless of whether you rely on a contract facility, you are responsible for assuring that drugs you produce are neither adulterated nor misbranded. [See 21 CFR 210.1(b), 21 CFR 200.10(b).]

FDA strongly recommends that your management undertake a comprehensive assessment of operations, including facility design, procedures, personnel, processes, maintenance, materials, and systems. In particular, this review should assess your aseptic processing operations. A third-party consultant with relevant sterile drug manufacturing expertise should assist you in conducting this comprehensive evaluation.

D. Conclusion

The violations cited in this letter are not intended to be an all-inclusive statement of violations at your facility. You are responsible for investigating and determining the causes of any violations and for preventing their recurrence or the occurrence of other violations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including FDA regulations.

You should take prompt action to address any violations. Failure to adequately address any violations may result in legal action without further notice, including, without limitation, seizure and injunction.

Within fifteen (15) working days of receipt of this letter, please notify this office in writing of the specific steps that you have taken to address any violations. Please include an explanation of each step being taken to prevent the recurrence of violations, as well as copies of related documentation. This letter notifies you of our concerns and provides you an opportunity to address them. If you believe your products are not in violation of the FDCA, include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. If you cannot completely address this matter within fifteen (15) working days, state the reason for the delay and the time within which you will do so.

All correspondence should refer to the Warning Letter Number above (# 724202) and include a subject line that clearly identifies the submission as a Response to Warning Letter. If you have questions regarding the contents of this letter, please contact compoundinginspections@fda.hhs.gov.

Sincerely,
/S/

Matthew J. Lash
Acting Director
Office of Compounding Quality and Compliance
Office of Compliance
Center for Drug Evaluation and Research

cc: Scott P. Luce, Chief Executive Officer

____________________

1 See Pub. L. No. 113-54, § 102(a), 127 Stat. 587, 587-588 (2013).

An outsourcing facility, which is defined in section 503B(d)(4) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 353b(d)(4)], is a facility at one geographic location or address that — (i) is engaged in the compounding of sterile drugs; (ii) has elected to register as an outsourcing facility; and (iii) complies with all of the requirements of this section. Outsourcing facilities must comply with other applicable provisions of the FDCA, including section 501(a)(2)(B) [21 U.S.C. § 351(a)(2)(B)], regarding current good manufacturing practice (CGMP), and section 501(a)(2)(A) [21 U.S.C. § 351(a)(2)(A)], regarding insanitary conditions. Generally, CGMP requirements for the preparation of drug products are established in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) parts 210 and 211.

B. Violations of the FDCA

Adulterated Drug Products

The FDA investigator collected evidence indicating that drug products intended or expected to be sterile were prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions, whereby they may have become contaminated with filth or rendered injurious to health, causing your drug products to be adulterated under section 501(a)(2)(A) of the FDCA. For example, the investigator collected evidence indicating that:

1. Your facility lacked routine and rigorous certification of the ISO 5 areas, including airflow visualization studies performed under dynamic conditions.

2. Your firm did not perform adequate product evaluation and take appropriate corrective action after microbial contamination was recovered within the ISO 5 aseptic processing area.

3. Your component control is not adequately designed or maintained to prevent contamination of product contact surfaces due to the presence of foreign (unusual) material between the stopper ribs of syringes.

4. Your compounding technicians and aseptic assistants employ poor practices which introduce risk of microbial contamination into the ISO 5 classified critical areas during production of drugs intended to be sterile.

For example, during the production of Fentanyl Citrate 2 mcg/mL Bupivacaine HCl 0.125% lot #1125035913 and/or Methadone HCl 10 mg/mL lot #1125035922, your compounding technicians:

a. Moved quickly in a critical area or in an area immediately adjacent to a critical area such that unidirectional airflow is likely to be disrupted.

b. Leaned into the hood, allowing their head and upper body to enter the ISO 5 classified critical area, thereby disrupting unidirectional airflow.

c. Blocked first pass air by placing gloved hands directly over the following:

i. Hanging IV bag ports when making sterile connections.

ii. The IV bag ports when disinfecting prior to filling.

iii. The open filled syringes and the syringe cap trays during the process of screwing caps onto the syringes.

d. Conducted aseptic operations on or directly above the hood deck surface in vertical flow hoods, which prevents unidirectional first air with minimal turbulence from surrounding aseptic operations during sterile connections and filling of drug products intended or expected to be sterile into open sterile containers.

e. Regularly rested their arms on the work surface of the hood during aseptic production. This practice may introduce contamination into the ISO 5 work area.

Additionally, your aseptic assistants:

a. Moved quickly in an area immediately adjacent to a critical area such that unidirectional airflow is likely to be disrupted.

b. Used disinfectant in a manner insufficient to achieve adequate levels of disinfection of materials, such as the IV bag ports, during transfer into the ISO 5 classified critical areas by spraying very quickly or from a significant distance or failing to treat both sides of the IV bags. Prior to disinfection, aseptic assistants regularly touched the IV bag ports in the ISO 7 area with their gloved hands.

5. Your environmental monitoring program lacks adequate routine environmental monitoring that captures data representative of aseptic production conditions. For example, during the production of Fentanyl Citrate 2 mcg/mL Bupivacaine HCl 0.125% lot #1125035913:

a. The active air sampler is placed to the far right of the hood instead of adjacent to the areas where aseptic operations occur, including the left and center portions of the ISO 5 classified hood.

b. Compounding technicians do not always carefully roll their individual fingers across the media touch plate during personnel monitoring. The compounding technician quickly touched each fingertip to the media plates instead of methodically rolling their fingertips.

6. Your firm failed to perform adequate airflow visualization studies under dynamic conditions to demonstrate unidirectional airflow within the ISO 5 area. Your airflow visualization studies are deficient because:

a. The studies do not clearly demonstrate that the airflow pattern sweeps over and away from the critical areas near and on the ISO 5 classified LAF hood work surface where aseptic operations occur. Instead, the smoke appears to arc out of the hood significantly higher than the critical area and then travel up toward the ceiling in the surrounding ISO 7 classified area.

b. In your most recent airflow visualization study VAL-25-044-FR, you indicated that (b)(4) people are allowed in ISO 7 (b)(4) Room (b)(4) during aseptic operations; however, the smoke study videos provided during the FDA inspection only include a maximum of (b)(4) people, and fail to demonstrate that airflow patterns inside the ISO 5 classified critical areas are not impacted by a large number of personnel moving inside cleanroom Room (b)(4).

The FDA investigator also collected evidence indicating CGMP violations at your facility, that caused your drug products to be adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FDCA. The violations include, for example:

1. Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures that are designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile, and that include validation of all aseptic and sterilization processes (21 CFR 211.113(b)).

2. Your firm failed to establish an adequate air supply filtered through high-efficiency particulate air filters under positive pressure in the aseptic processing areas (21 CFR 211.42(c)(10)(iii)).

3. Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192).

4. Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures designed to assure that components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling, and drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)).

5. Your firm failed to establish adequate written responsibilities and procedures applicable to the quality control unit and to follow written procedures applicable to the quality control unit (21 CFR 211.22(d)). Specifically, our review of the data collected during the inspection revealed that your firm does not maintain the production video recordings which are used to determine root causes and corrective actions during investigations. For example, after recovering microbial contamination inside the ISO 5 classified critical area during the production of Ketamine HCl 10 mg/mL lot 1125035065, your Quality Unit evaluated the production video recording as part of excursion investigation EXC-2025-0045 to examine aseptic practices for potential root causes. However, instead of retaining the video recording as a quality related document, you only retained still images. Your Chief Quality Officer stated that video recordings are kept for approximately (b)(4) before being overwritten.

Outsourcing facilities must comply with CGMP requirements under section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FDCA. FDA’s regulations regarding CGMP requirements for the preparation of drug products have been established in 21 CFR parts 210 and 211. FDA intends to promulgate more specific CGMP regulations for outsourcing facilities. FDA has issued a revised draft guidance, Current Good Manufacturing Practice — Guidance for Human Drug Compounding Outsourcing Facilities under Section 503B of the FD&C Act. This draft guidance, when finalized, will describe FDA’s expectations regarding outsourcing facilities and the CGMP requirements in 21 CFR parts 210 and 211 until more specific CGMP regulations for outsourcing facilities are promulgated.

Under section 301(a) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(a)], the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce of any drug that is adulterated is a prohibited act. Further, it is also a prohibited act under section 301(k) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(k)] to do any act with respect to a drug, if such act is done while the drug is held for sale after shipment in interstate commerce and results in the drug being adulterated.

C. Corrective Actions

We have reviewed your facility’s responses to the Form FDA 483 dated November 21, 2025, and December 31, 2025.

Some of your corrective actions appear adequate. However, we are unable to fully evaluate some of your corrective actions due to lack of adequate supporting documentation:

1. Although you stated that you performed airflow visualization studies in all (b)(4) hoods, you did not clearly demonstrate that these studies were performed in all (b)(4) hoods during the most recent airflow visualization assessment, performed in 2025. Additionally, while you concluded that the hoods are identical and therefore functionally equivalent, this approach does not account for potential variations in the HEPA filter performance, for example, resulting from particulate accumulation over time, nor the impact of physical placement of hoods within the room—including proximity to doors, return vents, and other environmental factors that may affect airflow where production activities are occurring.

Some of your corrective actions appear deficient:

1. You did not demonstrate that the probable root cause of inadequate material sanitization had no impact on the released portions of the batch associated with microbial excursions in the ISO 5 classified areas during production. You indicated both in your investigations and in your response that your material sanitization process is robust, but also concluded that the microbial contamination was most likely due to inadequate material sanitization.

You failed to demonstrate that microbial contamination was not present in the materials associated with the released portions of the batch. You did not demonstrate that the material sanitization process for the released portions of the batches did not include the same deficiencies as the material sanitization for the rejected portion of the batch. Further, you failed to initiate any corrective and preventative action plans to determine whether you need to improve your material sanitization process to prevent reoccurrence.

2. It appears that your visual inspection system is inadequate because you classify particulate defects as major and therefore only characterize and investigate the observed particles when the defect rate is above the major defect threshold of (b)(4)%. Extrinsic particulates should be classified as critical, and the intrinsic particulates should be evaluated based on multiple factors, including particle size and route of administration, to determine the appropriate defect classification. Your SOP ILP-001-LR, Product Inspection and Defect Classification, states, “If a DRL (Defect Rate Limit) threshold is exceeded related to ‘Particulate/material in solution,’ the particulate/material must be identified during the event.” According to your visual inspection data, you detected between (b)(4) and (b)(4) particles in (b)(4) separate lots between April 2025 and September 2025, only (b)(4) lots of which exceeded the (b)(4)% threshold for major defects. According to your Deviation log, only (b)(4) defect incidents were investigated between April 2025 and September 2025, and these were related to any Defect Rate Limit Threshold Exceedance, not just those involving particles. Therefore, you do not have an adequate system in place to ensure that you identify and appropriately investigate contaminating particles.

3. You did not commit to revising the minor defect classification for “[f]oreign (unusual) material, e.g., cardboard trapped between stopper ribs” to account for the criticality of the foreign material. While you noted that any units exhibiting this defect are rejected, the defect rate limit applied to minor defects ((b)(4)%) is not appropriate for adequately investigating, trending, and performing corrective actions, as necessary, to mitigate this contamination risk.

You did not provide adequate documentation to demonstrate that foreign materials are contained within the ribs of the syringe stoppers in non-product-contact area and will not pose contamination risks to the drug product. In addition, the syringe filling process demonstrates that the foreign material does come into contact with product-contact area of the syringes. For example, any cardboard particles trapped within the syringe ribs may be pressed against the inner syringe wall during filling, potentially introducing particles onto a surface that subsequently contacts the drug product solution.

In addition to the issues discussed above, you should note that CGMP requires the implementation of quality oversight and controls over the manufacture of drugs, including the safety of raw materials, materials used in drug manufacturing, and finished drug products. See section 501 of the FDCA. If you choose to contract with a laboratory to perform some functions required by CGMP, it is essential that you select a qualified contractor and that you maintain sufficient oversight of the contractor’s operations to ensure that it is fully CGMP compliant. Regardless of whether you rely on a contract facility, you are responsible for assuring that drugs you produce are neither adulterated nor misbranded. [See 21 CFR 210.1(b), 21 CFR 200.10(b).]

FDA strongly recommends that your management undertake a comprehensive assessment of operations, including facility design, procedures, personnel, processes, maintenance, materials, and systems. In particular, this review should assess your aseptic processing operations. A third-party consultant with relevant sterile drug manufacturing expertise should assist you in conducting this comprehensive evaluation.

D. Conclusion

The violations cited in this letter are not intended to be an all-inclusive statement of violations at your facility. You are responsible for investigating and determining the causes of any violations and for preventing their recurrence or the occurrence of other violations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including FDA regulations.

You should take prompt action to address any violations. Failure to adequately address any violations may result in legal action without further notice, including, without limitation, seizure and injunction.

Within fifteen (15) working days of receipt of this letter, please notify this office in writing of the specific steps that you have taken to address any violations. Please include an explanation of each step being taken to prevent the recurrence of violations, as well as copies of related documentation. This letter notifies you of our concerns and provides you an opportunity to address them. If you believe your products are not in violation of the FDCA, include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. If you cannot completely address this matter within fifteen (15) working days, state the reason for the delay and the time within which you will do so.

All correspondence should refer to the Warning Letter Number above (# 724202) and include a subject line that clearly identifies the submission as a Response to Warning Letter. If you have questions regarding the contents of this letter, please contact compoundinginspections@fda.hhs.gov.

Sincerely,
/S/

Matthew J. Lash
Acting Director
Office of Compounding Quality and Compliance
Office of Compliance
Center for Drug Evaluation and Research

cc: Scott P. Luce, Chief Executive Officer

____________________

1 See Pub. L. No. 113-54, § 102(a), 127 Stat. 587, 587-588 (2013).",

Find a federal candidate's FEC candidate ID and principal campaign committee before asking for totals, filings or independent expenditures.

cursor.description: next_cursor from the previous call. Keep the same filters and sort. Pattern: ^last_index=[A-Za-z0-9.:_-]{1,40}(&[a-z_]+=[A-Za-z0-9.:_-]{1,40}){0,5}$|^[a-z_]+=[A-Za-z0-9.:_-]{1,40}(&[a-z_]+=[A-Za-z0-9.:_-]{1,40}){1,5}$.

cycle.description: Two-year election cycle, named by its even year: 2024 covers 2023-2024.

most_recent.description: Only the latest version of each expenditure (excludes superseded amendments).

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote:

The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955.

Implementation Note issued September 16, 2026

The Federal Reserve Implements Improvements and Streamlines the Borrower-in-Custody Program
The Fed's Discount Window: 1990 to the Present

response.location: At the 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York
response.speaker: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson
response.text:
Thank you for the opportunity to speak at the Treasury Market Conference. Today I will discuss modernization of the Federal Reserve's discount window and some implications of that modernization for Treasury market functioning.1

As this group knows well, the Federal Reserve's discount window lending program provides liquidity to banks.2 Banks access discount window liquidity overwhelmingly through primary credit borrowing, which is offered on a "no questions asked" basis. The discount window is as old as the Federal Reserve itself, which will be 113 years old in December.3 Over its long history, the Federal Reserve has used the discount window to support the liquidity and stability of the banking system and to implement monetary policy. For the discount window to continue to do so, it is important that the discount window evolves with the banking and financial system. That is why the staff at the Board of Governors and at each Federal Reserve Bank have worked diligently over the past several years to enhance discount window operations. The continuing efforts to modernize the discount window ensure a more efficient, accessible source of liquidity that banks can access quickly and without hesitation when needed.

Of course, the Treasury market arguably is as old as our country itself, with the origins of federal debt dating back to the Revolutionary War.4 That said, the beginnings of the modern Treasury market are more directly traced to World War I.5 Over the past century, the Treasury market has evolved into one of the deepest and most liquid markets in the world.

In the Federal Reserve System, there is an array of responsibilities among Reserve Banks and the Board regarding the discount window. The Reserve Banks operate the discount window in their Districts, and the Board provides oversight and establishes policy through regulations and guidance to Reserve Banks. Because policy and operations are closely intertwined, the Board coordinates extensively with Reserve Bank leadership and staff on discount window matters. I have the privilege of serving as the Oversight Governor for the Division of Monetary Affairs. In that capacity, I oversee the Board's work on discount window policy.

Today I will discuss the progress we have made in recent years to further modernize the discount window. Then, I will speak briefly about the role of Treasury securities as collateral for discount window loans. But, first, I cannot overemphasize that modernizing discount window operations is a true Systemwide effort and that teamwork is key. While notable strides have been made, there is still important work to do. I look forward to seeing continued improvements in discount window operations in the coming years.

Three Dimensions of Discount Window Modernization Now, I will move on to what we are doing at the Federal Reserve to modernize the discount window to meet 21st-century banking needs.6 Over the past few years, the System has conducted extensive outreach to banks and other stakeholders to understand better their experiences with the discount window, including the Board's issuance of a request for information (RFI) on discount window operations in 2024. This RFI complemented the ongoing conversations with the public that occur at all levels and in multiple corners of the Federal Reserve System, such as Ask the Fed® sessions and Reserve Bank outreach events. We have made progress in addressing feedback received through these various channels as part of our modernization efforts and are implementing improvements so banks can benefit as quickly as possible.

I think of the System's work on discount window modernization along three dimensions: business process improvements, automation enhancements, and coordination with the Federal Home Loan Banks (FHLBs).

First, ongoing business process improvements have been supporting better efficiency and standardization. Reserve Banks have focused on providing banks with more efficient access to the discount window. In terms of standardization, all Districts work within the same collateral framework, use common loan valuation models and processing technology, and accept electronic signatures. Earlier this month, the Reserve Banks took an important step to further simplify and streamline how banks pledge loans as collateral.7 These changes allow eligible institutions to pledge several different loan types to maximize liquidity while maintaining possession of the collateral. The recently enacted changes include simplified forms, faster enrollment, automated pledged loan lists, and centralized resources so that institutions can easily find the information they need. These process improvements further enhance consistency in collateral administration across the 12 Reserve Banks while still maintaining robust risk-management practices.

Second, we have enhanced the discount window user experience. In 2024, the System launched Discount Window Direct (DWD), a self-service online portal that allows banks to request loans, make payments, view loan and collateral information, and submit loan collateral files electronically. Since the portal's launch, users have reported that it is now faster, easier, and more efficient to borrow from the discount window. Today, over 60 percent of discount window loan requests are submitted through DWD. The portal also includes a messaging feature that allows banks to directly message their local Reserve Bank in lieu of a phone call. Faster, more efficient discount window access gives banks greater certainty as they manage fast-moving liquidity needs. As adoption grows and new features are added, this technology will continue improving the discount window experience.

Third, and very important, is our collaboration with the FHLBs. As many of you may know, the FHLBs are important liquidity providers to banking organizations, and both the Federal Reserve and FHLB Systems share the goal of supporting the stability and resilience of the U.S. banking system. Given the increased speed with which liquidity can now move, a key focus of ours has been reducing the time it takes to re-allocate collateral by enhancing interoperability between Reserve Banks and FHLBs.

Efforts to date have focused on improving preparedness through measures that support coordination and collaboration between Reserve Banks and FHLBs—this initiative includes reinforcing relationships, establishing back-end operational arrangements and documentation, and developing processes that enable Reserve Banks and FHLBs to work together more effectively. We and our FHLB partners believe our ongoing efforts and continued commitment to this coordination put us in a much better position than three years ago by meaningfully improving our processes and strengthening relationships and engagement between the two Systems.

On a personal note, I have had an opportunity to engage with the FHLB presidents and other leaders in the FHLB System, and I appreciate greatly their ongoing collaboration and support as we continue to work together on interoperability. This engagement is not just about crisis preparedness—it is also about building lasting, more effective institutional partnerships.

Of course, the Federal Reserve's work on enhancements to the discount window is a continuous process. In over a century, the discount window has evolved from a physical teller window at a Reserve Bank that a bank representative had to visit to an online portal that permits a bank to request a loan with a few clicks. We are living through an era of rapid economic and technological transformation, and it will be crucial that the discount window continues to evolve and respond to our ever-changing environment. The modernization efforts I have described make discount window borrowing faster and less operationally burdensome. These improvements, I believe, help reduce the frictions that may make banks hesitant to use the window when they are healthy and reinforce overall confidence in the banking system. Our work is not done, but I remain committed to working with my colleagues throughout the Federal Reserve System to do just that.

Treasury Securities as Discount Window Collateral This commitment brings me to an increasingly important dimension of discount window operations. A well-functioning Treasury market is essential to the stability and the efficiency of the financial system and the economy more broadly. The U.S. Treasury market serves as the foundation for pricing risk across all asset classes, facilitating the efficient allocation of capital throughout our economy. In this context, the discount window supports Treasury market resilience in important ways. By providing banks with a reliable source of liquidity, the discount window serves as a shock absorber during periods of market stress by reducing the risk of forced sales of Treasury securities. Moreover, the discount window's stabilizing influence extends to broader money markets. By alleviating funding pressures at depository institutions, the discount window helps ensure the smooth functioning of key short-term funding markets—including the repurchase agreement (repo) market and the federal funds market. This dynamic, in turn, supports Treasury market liquidity.

Institutions holding Treasury securities in their Fedwire Securities accounts can quickly transfer them to their discount window pledge account even late in the day. For institutions that have arrangements in place, this means that pledging Treasury collateral and receiving a same-day loan are straightforward and efficient. This speed and ease of access matter for market functioning, particularly when banks active in the Treasury market need liquidity quickly. The COVID-19 crisis demonstrated this predicament clearly. In March 2020, when the Treasury market experienced severe dysfunction, we saw a sharp increase in Treasury securities pledged to the Federal Reserve to secure potential discount window loans. The Federal Reserve's ability to accept Treasury securities quickly and to provide banks with the option of obtaining reserves if they were needed proved critical.8

The discount window also helps respond to sudden tightening in money markets, supporting the Federal Reserve's monetary policy implementation and complementing the standing repo operations in relieving funding market pressures. When pressures emerge in money markets, banks can turn to the discount window rather than borrowing at rates above the Federal Reserve's target range. Indeed, we have recently seen more use of the discount window amid periods associated with temporary upward pressure on money market rates, such as those observed at quarter-ends.

The interaction between the Treasury market and the discount window that I have described underscores why maintaining a robust and effective discount window framework is not merely about banks, but critically important for financial stability more broadly.

Conclusion As I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, the Federal Reserve's ability to lend to banks through the discount window dates to the System's founding and is one of our core functions. This liquidity provision serves a variety of purposes: it facilitates the ability of banks to lend to households and businesses and supports other financial market participants during stress or volatile market conditions. It is particularly important for Treasury markets that banks can serve as a source of strength for market functioning. The discount window's acceptance of Treasury securities as collateral with same-day value helps make this stability possible.

Today the discount window remains ready to lend smoothly and effectively to banks when needed. The modernization efforts I have discussed will ensure that the discount window supports individual banking institutions and broader market resilience well into the future. To be sure, we cannot be complacent when it comes to the discount window. Ultimately, I believe that the continued success of the discount window, as with many endeavors, lies with the ongoing partnership and dedication of various stakeholders within the Federal Reserve System and those external to it, including many of you here today. Working together, we will continue to fulfill the fundamental purpose of the discount window as established over a century ago—and thereby achieve the best outcomes for the American people.

Thank you.

1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text

2. See Philip N. Jefferson (2024), "A History of the Fed's Discount Window: 1913–2000," speech delivered at Davidson College, Davidson, N.C., October 8. Return to text

3. See Federal Reserve Act, Pub. L. No. 63-43, 38 Stat. 251 (December 23, 1913). Return to text

4. See Richard Sylla and David J. Cowen (2018), Alexander Hamilton on Finance, Credit, and Debt (New York: Columbia University Press). Return to text

5. See Kenneth D. Garbade (2012), Birth of a Market: The U.S. Treasury Securities Market from the Great War to the Great Depression (Cambridge: MIT Press). Return to text

6. See Federal Reserve Discount Window (2026), "Discount Window Modernization," webpage. Return to text

7. See Federal Reserve Discount Window (2026), "The Federal Reserve Implements Improvements and Streamlines the Borrower-in-Custody Program," webpage, September 8. Return to text

8. For a discussion of the discount window's role in recent stress episodes, see Philip N. Jefferson (2024) "The Fed's Discount Window: 1990 to the Present," speech delivered at the Charlotte Economics Club, Charlotte, N.C., October 9. Return to text

# Fixed reference example. Playground inputs do not update this sample.
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.aisa.one/apis/v1/firecrawl-alexandria/federalreserve-gov/central-bank-communications/speech \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "alexandria": {
    "provider": "federalreserve-gov",
    "capability": "central-bank-communications/speech",
    "options": {
      "request": {
        "slug": "jefferson20260922a"
      },
      "response": {
        "date": "September 22, 2026",
        "kind": "speech",
        "last_update": "September 22, 2026",
        "links": [
          {
            "text": "A History of the Fed'"'"'s Discount Window: 1913–2000",
            "url": "https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/jefferson20241008a.htm"
          },
          {
            "text": "Discount Window Modernization",
            "url": "https://www.frbdiscountwindow.org/pages/general-information/dw_modernization"
          },
          {
            "text": "The Federal Reserve Implements Improvements and Streamlines the Borrower-in-Custody Program",
            "url": "https://www.frbdiscountwindow.org/articles/2026/09/04/18/05/bic_standards_announcement_20260908"
          },
          {
            "text": "The Fed'"'"'s Discount Window: 1990 to the Present",
            "url": "https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/jefferson20241009a.htm"
          }
        ],
        "live_url": "https://www.newyorkfed.org/newsevents/events/markets/2026/0922-2026",
        "location": "At the 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York",
        "observed_at_ms": 1790122887332,
        "pdf_url": "https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/files/jefferson20260922a.pdf",
        "slug": "jefferson20260922a",
        "speaker": "Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson",
        "text": "Thank you for the opportunity to speak at the Treasury Market Conference. Today I will discuss modernization of the Federal Reserve'"'"'s discount window and some implications of that modernization for Treasury market functioning.1

As this group knows well, the Federal Reserve'"'"'s discount window lending program provides liquidity to banks.2 Banks access discount window liquidity overwhelmingly through primary credit borrowing, which is offered on a "no questions asked" basis. The discount window is as old as the Federal Reserve itself, which will be 113 years old in December.3 Over its long history, the Federal Reserve has used the discount window to support the liquidity and stability of the banking system and to implement monetary policy. For the discount window to continue to do so, it is important that the discount window evolves with the banking and financial system. That is why the staff at the Board of Governors and at each Federal Reserve Bank have worked diligently over the past several years to enhance discount window operations. The continuing efforts to modernize the discount window ensure a more efficient, accessible source of liquidity that banks can access quickly and without hesitation when needed.

Of course, the Treasury market arguably is as old as our country itself, with the origins of federal debt dating back to the Revolutionary War.4 That said, the beginnings of the modern Treasury market are more directly traced to World War I.5 Over the past century, the Treasury market has evolved into one of the deepest and most liquid markets in the world.

In the Federal Reserve System, there is an array of responsibilities among Reserve Banks and the Board regarding the discount window. The Reserve Banks operate the discount window in their Districts, and the Board provides oversight and establishes policy through regulations and guidance to Reserve Banks. Because policy and operations are closely intertwined, the Board coordinates extensively with Reserve Bank leadership and staff on discount window matters. I have the privilege of serving as the Oversight Governor for the Division of Monetary Affairs. In that capacity, I oversee the Board'"'"'s work on discount window policy.

Today I will discuss the progress we have made in recent years to further modernize the discount window. Then, I will speak briefly about the role of Treasury securities as collateral for discount window loans. But, first, I cannot overemphasize that modernizing discount window operations is a true Systemwide effort and that teamwork is key. While notable strides have been made, there is still important work to do. I look forward to seeing continued improvements in discount window operations in the coming years.

Three Dimensions of Discount Window Modernization Now, I will move on to what we are doing at the Federal Reserve to modernize the discount window to meet 21st-century banking needs.6 Over the past few years, the System has conducted extensive outreach to banks and other stakeholders to understand better their experiences with the discount window, including the Board'"'"'s issuance of a request for information (RFI) on discount window operations in 2024. This RFI complemented the ongoing conversations with the public that occur at all levels and in multiple corners of the Federal Reserve System, such as Ask the Fed® sessions and Reserve Bank outreach events. We have made progress in addressing feedback received through these various channels as part of our modernization efforts and are implementing improvements so banks can benefit as quickly as possible.

I think of the System'"'"'s work on discount window modernization along three dimensions: business process improvements, automation enhancements, and coordination with the Federal Home Loan Banks (FHLBs).

First, ongoing business process improvements have been supporting better efficiency and standardization. Reserve Banks have focused on providing banks with more efficient access to the discount window. In terms of standardization, all Districts work within the same collateral framework, use common loan valuation models and processing technology, and accept electronic signatures. Earlier this month, the Reserve Banks took an important step to further simplify and streamline how banks pledge loans as collateral.7 These changes allow eligible institutions to pledge several different loan types to maximize liquidity while maintaining possession of the collateral. The recently enacted changes include simplified forms, faster enrollment, automated pledged loan lists, and centralized resources so that institutions can easily find the information they need. These process improvements further enhance consistency in collateral administration across the 12 Reserve Banks while still maintaining robust risk-management practices.

Second, we have enhanced the discount window user experience. In 2024, the System launched Discount Window Direct (DWD), a self-service online portal that allows banks to request loans, make payments, view loan and collateral information, and submit loan collateral files electronically. Since the portal'"'"'s launch, users have reported that it is now faster, easier, and more efficient to borrow from the discount window. Today, over 60 percent of discount window loan requests are submitted through DWD. The portal also includes a messaging feature that allows banks to directly message their local Reserve Bank in lieu of a phone call. Faster, more efficient discount window access gives banks greater certainty as they manage fast-moving liquidity needs. As adoption grows and new features are added, this technology will continue improving the discount window experience.

Third, and very important, is our collaboration with the FHLBs. As many of you may know, the FHLBs are important liquidity providers to banking organizations, and both the Federal Reserve and FHLB Systems share the goal of supporting the stability and resilience of the U.S. banking system. Given the increased speed with which liquidity can now move, a key focus of ours has been reducing the time it takes to re-allocate collateral by enhancing interoperability between Reserve Banks and FHLBs.

Efforts to date have focused on improving preparedness through measures that support coordination and collaboration between Reserve Banks and FHLBs—this initiative includes reinforcing relationships, establishing back-end operational arrangements and documentation, and developing processes that enable Reserve Banks and FHLBs to work together more effectively. We and our FHLB partners believe our ongoing efforts and continued commitment to this coordination put us in a much better position than three years ago by meaningfully improving our processes and strengthening relationships and engagement between the two Systems.

On a personal note, I have had an opportunity to engage with the FHLB presidents and other leaders in the FHLB System, and I appreciate greatly their ongoing collaboration and support as we continue to work together on interoperability. This engagement is not just about crisis preparedness—it is also about building lasting, more effective institutional partnerships.

Of course, the Federal Reserve'"'"'s work on enhancements to the discount window is a continuous process. In over a century, the discount window has evolved from a physical teller window at a Reserve Bank that a bank representative had to visit to an online portal that permits a bank to request a loan with a few clicks. We are living through an era of rapid economic and technological transformation, and it will be crucial that the discount window continues to evolve and respond to our ever-changing environment. The modernization efforts I have described make discount window borrowing faster and less operationally burdensome. These improvements, I believe, help reduce the frictions that may make banks hesitant to use the window when they are healthy and reinforce overall confidence in the banking system. Our work is not done, but I remain committed to working with my colleagues throughout the Federal Reserve System to do just that.

Treasury Securities as Discount Window Collateral This commitment brings me to an increasingly important dimension of discount window operations. A well-functioning Treasury market is essential to the stability and the efficiency of the financial system and the economy more broadly. The U.S. Treasury market serves as the foundation for pricing risk across all asset classes, facilitating the efficient allocation of capital throughout our economy. In this context, the discount window supports Treasury market resilience in important ways. By providing banks with a reliable source of liquidity, the discount window serves as a shock absorber during periods of market stress by reducing the risk of forced sales of Treasury securities. Moreover, the discount window'"'"'s stabilizing influence extends to broader money markets. By alleviating funding pressures at depository institutions, the discount window helps ensure the smooth functioning of key short-term funding markets—including the repurchase agreement (repo) market and the federal funds market. This dynamic, in turn, supports Treasury market liquidity.

Institutions holding Treasury securities in their Fedwire Securities accounts can quickly transfer them to their discount window pledge account even late in the day. For institutions that have arrangements in place, this means that pledging Treasury collateral and receiving a same-day loan are straightforward and efficient. This speed and ease of access matter for market functioning, particularly when banks active in the Treasury market need liquidity quickly. The COVID-19 crisis demonstrated this predicament clearly. In March 2020, when the Treasury market experienced severe dysfunction, we saw a sharp increase in Treasury securities pledged to the Federal Reserve to secure potential discount window loans. The Federal Reserve'"'"'s ability to accept Treasury securities quickly and to provide banks with the option of obtaining reserves if they were needed proved critical.8

The discount window also helps respond to sudden tightening in money markets, supporting the Federal Reserve'"'"'s monetary policy implementation and complementing the standing repo operations in relieving funding market pressures. When pressures emerge in money markets, banks can turn to the discount window rather than borrowing at rates above the Federal Reserve'"'"'s target range. Indeed, we have recently seen more use of the discount window amid periods associated with temporary upward pressure on money market rates, such as those observed at quarter-ends.

The interaction between the Treasury market and the discount window that I have described underscores why maintaining a robust and effective discount window framework is not merely about banks, but critically important for financial stability more broadly.

Conclusion As I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, the Federal Reserve'"'"'s ability to lend to banks through the discount window dates to the System'"'"'s founding and is one of our core functions. This liquidity provision serves a variety of purposes: it facilitates the ability of banks to lend to households and businesses and supports other financial market participants during stress or volatile market conditions. It is particularly important for Treasury markets that banks can serve as a source of strength for market functioning. The discount window'"'"'s acceptance of Treasury securities as collateral with same-day value helps make this stability possible.

Today the discount window remains ready to lend smoothly and effectively to banks when needed. The modernization efforts I have discussed will ensure that the discount window supports individual banking institutions and broader market resilience well into the future. To be sure, we cannot be complacent when it comes to the discount window. Ultimately, I believe that the continued success of the discount window, as with many endeavors, lies with the ongoing partnership and dedication of various stakeholders within the Federal Reserve System and those external to it, including many of you here today. Working together, we will continue to fulfill the fundamental purpose of the discount window as established over a century ago—and thereby achieve the best outcomes for the American people.

Thank you.

1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text

2. See Philip N. Jefferson (2024), "A History of the Fed'"'"'s Discount Window: 1913–2000," speech delivered at Davidson College, Davidson, N.C., October 8. Return to text

3. See Federal Reserve Act, Pub. L. No. 63-43, 38 Stat. 251 (December 23, 1913). Return to text

4. See Richard Sylla and David J. Cowen (2018), Alexander Hamilton on Finance, Credit, and Debt (New York: Columbia University Press). Return to text

5. See Kenneth D. Garbade (2012), Birth of a Market: The U.S. Treasury Securities Market from the Great War to the Great Depression (Cambridge: MIT Press). Return to text

6. See Federal Reserve Discount Window (2026), "Discount Window Modernization," webpage. Return to text

7. See Federal Reserve Discount Window (2026), "The Federal Reserve Implements Improvements and Streamlines the Borrower-in-Custody Program," webpage, September 8. Return to text

8. For a discussion of the discount window'"'"'s role in recent stress episodes, see Philip N. Jefferson (2024) "The Fed'"'"'s Discount Window: 1990 to the Present," speech delivered at the Charlotte Economics Club, Charlotte, N.C., October 9. Return to text",
        "title": "Discount Window Modernization and Treasury Market Functioning",
        "url": "https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/jefferson20260922a.htm"
      },
      "recordedAt": "2026-09-23"
    }
  },
  "zeroDataRetention": false
}'

post.description:
List recent policy speeches or testimony by a given official or in a date range and get the slug to pass to `speech`.

<!-- aisa-pricing:start -->
按用量计费；默认请求预估费用：$0.0005 USD（不是固定价格）。 声明的单位费率：每 firecrawl_credit $0.0001 USD。 最终费用以账户适用价格及实际结算为准。
<!-- aisa-pricing:end -->

from.description: Earliest date to include, YYYY-MM-DD. Pattern: ^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$.

offset.description: Rows to skip; pass the previous page's `next_offset` to continue.

query.description: Case-insensitive substring matched against the title (and, for speeches, speaker and location).

speaker.description: Case-insensitive substring of the speaker line as the site prints it, e.g. `Jefferson`, `Vice Chair`, `Warsh`.

to.description: Latest date to include, YYYY-MM-DD. Pattern: ^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$.

items.location: At the 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York
items.speaker: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson
items.title: Discount Window Modernization and Treasury Market Functioning

default.description: Error response; upstream passthrough responses may use provider formats

fields.description: FIPS three-digit numeric code used to identify counties and county equivalents in the United States, the District of Columbia, US territories, outlying areas of the US and freely associated states. Please note that Indian Reservations are not counties and thus will not have a FIPS county code, please utilize the placeCode field instead. If the designation is made for the entire state, this value will be 000 as multiple (all) counties cannot be entered.

post.description:
Find local disaster recovery contacts (aging services, crisis counseling, housing, legal aid, ...) for a specific state or territory such as `american-samoa`, `commonwealth-northern-mariana-islands` or `virgin-islands`.

<!-- aisa-pricing:start -->
按用量计费；默认请求预估费用：$0.0005 USD（不是固定价格）。 声明的单位费率：每 firecrawl_credit $0.0001 USD。 最终费用以账户适用价格及实际结算为准。
<!-- aisa-pricing:end -->

category_contains.description: Optional case-insensitive substring filter on the Category cell, e.g. `Housing`, `Crisis`, `Legal`. Without it every row is returned.

slug.description: Directory page slug from `list_referral_directories`, e.g. `american-samoa`, `commonwealth-northern-mariana-islands`, `virgin-islands`, `guam`, `puerto-rico`, `texas`. Pattern: ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$.

url.description: Alternative to `slug`: a pasted fema.gov referral directory URL.

fields.description: Optional column selection for `record.fields` (names as in NRIDataDictionary.csv, e.g. RISK_SCORE, WFIR_RISKR, IFLD_EALT); the identity columns are always present at the record's top level. Without it every column of the row is returned (465-476 per row).

id.description: NRI_ID (C30031, T30031000100, S30), the bare FIPS (30031, 30031000100, 30), a USPS state code (MT) for states, or the OID_ row number for tribal tables. Pattern: ^[A-Za-z0-9]+$.

release.description: Release path segment under /about/reports-and-data/openfema/nri/. FEMA serves only the current release (v120 = NRI v1.20, December 2025; v119 is a 404), so leave the default unless a newer release is published. Pattern: ^v[0-9]{3}$.

table.description: Which NRI table: `states` (56 rows), `counties` (3,232), `tribal_counties` (1,232 county x tribal-area rows), `tribal_tracts` (3,364 tract x tribal-area rows) or `tracts` (~85,155 census tracts, 634 MB, read by byte range).

post.description:
Bulk collection of county, tract, state or tribal risk rows (RISK_*, EAL_*, SOVI_*, RESL_* and the 18 hazard blocks). Use `fields` to keep pages small; use nri_get for one row.

<!-- aisa-pricing:start -->
按用量计费；默认请求预估费用：$0.0005 USD（不是固定价格）。 声明的单位费率：每 firecrawl_credit $0.0001 USD。 最终费用以账户适用价格及实际结算为准。
<!-- aisa-pricing:end -->

cursor.description: `next_cursor` of the previous page (opaque, pinned to the file MD5).

fields.description: Optional column selection for `record.fields` (names as in NRIDataDictionary.csv, e.g. RISK_SCORE, WFIR_RISKR, IFLD_EALT); the identity columns are always present at the record's top level. Without it every column of the row is returned (465-476 per row).

limit.description: Rows per page for the four one-fetch tables.

page_bytes.description: Tracts only: bytes per Range request (256 KiB to 24 MiB; about 130 rows per MiB).

release.description: Release path segment under /about/reports-and-data/openfema/nri/. FEMA serves only the current release (v120 = NRI v1.20, December 2025; v119 is a 404), so leave the default unless a newer release is published. Pattern: ^v[0-9]{3}$.

state.description: Keep only one state or territory: USPS code (`MT`) or STATEFIPS (`30`). Not available on `tracts` (no state index in a byte-range read).

table.description: Which NRI table: `states` (56 rows), `counties` (3,232), `tribal_counties` (1,232 county x tribal-area rows), `tribal_tracts` (3,364 tract x tribal-area rows) or `tracts` (~85,155 census tracts, 634 MB, read by byte range).

default.description: Error response; upstream passthrough responses may use provider formats

x-aisa-response-pending.reason: public success response has no authoritative payload declaration

declaration_type.description: Declaration type code: DR (major disaster), EM (emergency), FM (fire management). Pattern: ^[A-Za-z]{2,3}$.

declared_before.description: Only declarations on or before this date (YYYY-MM-DD). Pattern: ^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$.

disaster_number.description: FEMA disaster number (e.g. 4931); returns that disaster's designated-area rows.

incident_type.description: Exact incident type as OpenFEMA states it, e.g. `Typhoon`, `Hurricane`, `Severe Storm`, `Fire`, `Flood`, `Biological`.

skip.description: Rows to skip (OpenFEMA $skip); pass the previous page's `next_skip`.

state.description: Two-letter state or territory code as OpenFEMA stores it (AS, MP, VI, GU, PR, TX, ...). Pattern: ^[A-Za-z]{2}$.

post.description:
Projected points and stat lines for a position in one NFL week, in a specific league's scoring.

<!-- aisa-pricing:start -->
按用量计费；默认请求预估费用：$0.0005 USD（不是固定价格）。 声明的单位费率：每 firecrawl_credit $0.0001 USD。 最终费用以账户适用价格及实际结算为准。
<!-- aisa-pricing:end -->

limit.description: Return only the top N players. Omit for the full list.

position.description: Position. The site publishes no weekly defense or IDP projections.

scoring.description: Scoring preset: FFToday STD, HALF or PPR, or the ESPN, Yahoo, FFPC, Underdog, CBS Sports, NFL.com or NFFC default league scoring. Default PPR.

season.description: Season year; requires week. Omit for the current season.

week.description: NFL week: 1-18, or 21-24 for the wild-card, divisional, conference and Super Bowl rounds. Omit for the site's current week. A week the site has not published is not_found.

default.description: Error response; upstream passthrough responses may use provider formats

x-aisa-response-pending.reason: public success response has no authoritative payload declaration

post.description:
Weekly start/sit order for a position.

<!-- aisa-pricing:start -->
按用量计费；默认请求预估费用：$0.0005 USD（不是固定价格）。 声明的单位费率：每 firecrawl_credit $0.0001 USD。 最终费用以账户适用价格及实际结算为准。
<!-- aisa-pricing:end -->

limit.description: Return only the top N players. Omit for the full list.

position.description: Position. DEF is team defense / special teams; DL, LB and DB are IDP.

season.description: Season year; requires week. Omit for the current season.

week.description: NFL week: 1-18, or 21-24 for the wild-card, divisional, conference and Super Bowl rounds. Omit for the site's current week. A week the site has not published is not_found.

default.description: Error response; upstream passthrough responses may use provider formats

x-aisa-response-pending.reason: public success response has no authoritative payload declaration

post.description:
Current hotspots around one place (an air base, a city, a park) rather than a whole file.

<!-- aisa-pricing:start -->
按用量计费；默认请求预估费用：$0.0005 USD（不是固定价格）。 声明的单位费率：每 firecrawl_credit $0.0001 USD。 最终费用以账户适用价格及实际结算为准。
<!-- aisa-pricing:end -->

area.description: `world` or `west,south,east,north` in decimal degrees (longitude -180..180, latitude -90..90, west < east, south < north). Pattern: ^(world|-?\d{1,3}(\.\d+)?,-?\d{1,2}(\.\d+)?,-?\d{1,3}(\.\d+)?,-?\d{1,2}(\.\d+)?)$.

date.description: Last day of the range, UTC. Keyed mode passes it to the API; keyless mode only accepts dates covered by the 7-day files. Pattern: ^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$.

day_range.description: Days of data ending at `date` (or now). Each day counts as one transaction against the key's 5000 per 10 minutes.

limit.description: Maximum records returned; `truncated` says when more matched.

map_key.description: FIRMS MAP_KEY (32 lowercase hex characters, free by email at /api/map_key/). Omit to use the keyless files. Pattern: ^[0-9a-f]{32}$.

source.description: FIRMS source product name as used by /api/area. Keyless mode maps the NRT products to the file families; the `_SP` archives need `map_key`.

default.description: Error response; upstream passthrough responses may use provider formats

x-aisa-response-pending.reason: public success response has no authoritative payload declaration

Collect every current detection of a sensor for a window and region; walk regions instead of Global to keep 7d files small.

<!-- aisa-pricing:start -->

cursor.description: `next_cursor` from the previous page. Omit for the first page; a cursor from another file or sensor is rejected.

limit.description: Maximum rows per page. Rows left in the fetched byte range are re-read on the next page.

page_bytes.description: Bytes fetched per page (one Range request). Default 4 MiB.

region.description: Default Global. landsat only publishes Canada and USA_contiguous_and_Hawaii.

summary_only.description: Count the rows of the page without returning them (records is empty).

default.description: Error response; upstream passthrough responses may use provider formats

<!-- aisa-pricing:end -->

region.description: File region stem (from /api/coordinates/all). Default Global.

sensor.description: File family (path segment under /data/active_fire/). Omitted: every sensor that publishes the region (landsat only publishes Canada and USA_contiguous_and_Hawaii).

window.description: Rolling window of the file. Omitted: all three.

post.description:
